subtopic_detail: Established valproate therapy discovered in the second trimester after the teratogenic window has passed
stem:
You are the obstetric physician registrar seeing a 26 year old woman at 22 weeks in an unplanned first pregnancy. She takes sodium valproate 800 mg twice daily for generalised tonic clonic epilepsy and has been seizure free for 4 years.

She did not know she was pregnant until 14 weeks and has not seen her neurologist since. She drives to work and cares for her grandmother three afternoons a week. She stopped her folic acid two years ago.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 84 beats per minute, blood pressure 106/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 percent in room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Neurological examination normal, symphysis fundal height 22 cm, foetal movements reported as normal
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, liver function tests and urea and electrolytes within normal limits, 20 week morphology ultrasound not yet performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of her antiseizure medication?

options.text: Stop sodium valproate today and start lamotrigine 25 mg twice daily
options.rationale: Abrupt withdrawal of an effective antiseizure medication risks seizure recurrence and status epilepticus, and maternal convulsive seizures cause foetal hypoxia, placental abruption and maternal death. Lamotrigine also requires slow titration over many weeks to avoid severe cutaneous reactions, so it cannot provide cover during the switch. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Halve the valproate dose now and review her in the clinic in 4 weeks
options.rationale: Dose reduction to limit foetal exposure makes sense only before organogenesis is complete, and the major malformation risk was determined in the first trimester which has already passed. Halving the dose now delivers the seizure risk of undertreatment without the malformation benefit that motivated it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Stop valproate and commence levetiracetam 500 mg twice daily today
options.rationale: Levetiracetam is a preferred agent when epilepsy treatment is planned before conception, but switching at 22 weeks exposes a woman who has been seizure free for 4 years to breakthrough seizures during cross titration. The teratogenic exposure that motivates the switch has already occurred and cannot be undone by changing agents now. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Continue the current dose and arrange urgent neurology and scan review
options.rationale: Once the first trimester has passed the dominant risk shifts from malformation to maternal seizures, so the established effective regimen is maintained and coordinated review is arranged. The detailed morphology ultrasound is overdue and is needed to look for neural tube, cardiac, facial and limb anomalies, and to plan neonatal care and counselling about neurodevelopmental follow up. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Add folic acid 5 mg daily and make no change to her antiseizure dose
options.rationale: Continuing the dose is right, but high dose folate prevents neural tube defects only when taken from before conception through the first trimester, since the neural tube closes by about 28 days after conception. Starting it at 22 weeks cannot provide that protection, and offering it as the intervention substitutes a gesture for the specialist review and anomaly scan she actually needs. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Sodium valproate is the most teratogenic antiseizure medication in common use, carrying a major congenital malformation rate of roughly 10 per cent at higher doses and a substantial risk of impaired neurodevelopment and autism spectrum disorder in exposed children, both of which are dose dependent. Because of this it should not be started in anyone who could become pregnant without a pregnancy prevention programme and documented counselling. When a pregnancy is already established beyond the first trimester, however, the calculus reverses: organogenesis is complete, the exposure cannot be undone, and the remaining modifiable risk is maternal seizures, which cause foetal hypoxia, trauma, abruption and sudden unexpected death in epilepsy. The management is therefore continuation with coordinated obstetric and neurology care, a detailed anomaly scan, vitamin K planning for the neonate and arrangements for neurodevelopmental follow up.
key_points: Valproate teratogenicity and neurodevelopmental risk are both dose dependent and determined in the first trimester
After the first trimester the dominant modifiable risk becomes maternal seizures
Never switch or withdraw an effective antiseizure medication abruptly in pregnancy
High dose folate protects only when taken from before conception through early pregnancy
A detailed morphology ultrasound and coordinated neurology review are the concrete actions
explanation.pearls: Antiseizure drug levels fall through pregnancy as volume of distribution and clearance rise, with lamotrigine and levetiracetam affected most markedly, so plan level monitoring each trimester and a postpartum dose reduction to avoid toxicity in the first weeks after birth.

subtopic_detail: Polyhydramnios at 32 weeks with a normal glucose tolerance test and appropriate foetal growth
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 33 year old woman at 32 weeks in her third pregnancy, referred because her abdomen has been measuring large for dates and she feels uncomfortably tight.

Her oral glucose tolerance test at 28 weeks was normal. Her blood group is O positive with a negative antibody screen. Her two previous pregnancies were uncomplicated and both babies weighed around 3.4 kg.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 88 beats per minute, blood pressure 114/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 percent in room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius, foetal heart rate 148 beats per minute
data_table.Examination: Symphysis fundal height 39 cm, uterus tense with foetal parts difficult to palpate, no uterine tenderness or activity, cervix long and closed on speculum examination
data_table.Ultrasound: Deepest vertical pool 10.4 cm, estimated foetal weight on the 55th centile, umbilical artery Doppler indices normal, no foetal ascites or skin oedema, placenta posterior and clear of the os

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Repeat the oral glucose tolerance test and check the HbA1c level
options.rationale: Maternal diabetes is the commonest identifiable cause of polyhydramnios and is worth reconsidering, but the tests would be expected to show macrosomia and accelerated growth rather than an estimated weight on the 55th centile. Repeating glucose testing alone leaves the structural causes unexamined. (Source: RANZCOG: Amniotic fluid abnormalities)

options.text: Arrange therapeutic amnioreduction to reduce the preterm birth risk
options.rationale: Amnioreduction is a symptomatic treatment reserved for severe polyhydramnios causing maternal respiratory compromise or intractable discomfort, and it carries risks of membrane rupture, abruption and infection. It is not used before the cause has been sought, and this woman has moderate rather than severe accumulation. (Source: RANZCOG: Amniotic fluid abnormalities)

options.text: Arrange a detailed ultrasound of foetal anatomy and the stomach bubble
options.rationale: Amniotic fluid volume from the second trimester onwards reflects foetal urine production balanced against foetal swallowing, so an excess with normal growth and normal Dopplers points towards impaired swallowing from a gastrointestinal, neurological or neuromuscular cause. An absent or small stomach bubble is the specific sign of oesophageal atresia, and identifying it before birth changes delivery planning, because these neonates must not be fed before the diagnosis is confirmed. (Source: RANZCOG: Amniotic fluid abnormalities)

options.text: Plan induction of labour at 37 weeks to avoid membrane rupture risk
options.rationale: Cord prolapse and abruption at membrane rupture are genuine concerns with a distended uterus and a high presenting part, and delivery planning follows once the cause is known. Committing to a date before the foetal anatomy has been assessed risks delivering a baby with an undiagnosed anomaly in a unit without neonatal surgical support. (Source: RANZCOG: Amniotic fluid abnormalities)

options.text: Measure the middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity this week
options.rationale: A raised middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity identifies foetal anaemia, which can cause polyhydramnios as part of hydrops from red cell alloimmunisation or parvovirus infection. The antibody screen is negative and there is no ascites or skin oedema, so hydrops is not the pattern here, and the measurement would be a narrow test for an unlikely cause. (Source: RANZCOG: Amniotic fluid abnormalities)

explanation.summary: Polyhydramnios complicates 1 to 2 per cent of pregnancies and is defined by a deepest vertical pool of 8 cm or more or an amniotic fluid index of 24 cm or more. About half of cases are idiopathic, but the identifiable causes divide neatly into increased foetal urine output, as in maternal diabetes, foetal anaemia and twin to twin transfusion, and reduced foetal swallowing, as in oesophageal or duodenal atresia, neuromuscular disorders and central nervous system anomalies. The evaluation therefore covers maternal glucose status, red cell antibodies and a detailed anatomical survey, with congenital infection serology added where relevant. Even after a negative workup, polyhydramnios carries increased risks of preterm birth, malpresentation, cord prolapse, abruption at membrane rupture and postpartum haemorrhage from uterine overdistension, so the birth plan is adjusted accordingly.
key_points: Deepest vertical pool 8 cm or more, or amniotic fluid index 24 cm or more, defines polyhydramnios
Causes split into increased urine output and reduced foetal swallowing
Normal growth with normal Dopplers shifts suspicion towards a swallowing or structural cause
An absent stomach bubble suggests oesophageal atresia and changes neonatal feeding plans
Uterine overdistension raises the risk of cord prolapse, abruption and postpartum haemorrhage
explanation.pearls: A neonate born after unexplained polyhydramnios should have a nasogastric tube passed and its position confirmed on radiograph before the first feed, because a tube coiling in the upper pouch confirms oesophageal atresia and prevents aspiration.

subtopic_detail: Postmenopausal bleeding on tamoxifen where the endometrial thickness threshold does not apply
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 63 year old woman who has had three episodes of light vaginal bleeding over the past two months. Her last menstrual period was 12 years ago.

She completed surgery and radiotherapy for an oestrogen receptor positive breast cancer 5 years ago and has taken tamoxifen 20 mg daily since. She takes no other hormonal preparation and has never used menopausal hormone therapy.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 26 kg/m2, vulva and vagina atrophic with no visible lesion, cervix smooth with no polyp or contact bleeding, uterus normal size and mobile, adnexae impalpable
data_table.Investigations: Transvaginal ultrasound reports endometrial thickness 7 mm with a heterogeneous appearance and subendometrial cystic spaces, both ovaries normal, cervical screening test negative for oncogenic HPV 8 months ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure her that a thickness below 8 mm excludes endometrial cancer
options.rationale: The endometrial thickness threshold used to exclude malignancy in postmenopausal bleeding is 4 mm, not 8 mm, and even that figure is validated only in women not taking tamoxifen. Applying any ultrasound cut-off to reassure a woman on tamoxifen misuses a test whose specificity collapses in this population. (Source: RANZCOG: Investigation of postmenopausal bleeding)

options.text: Repeat the transvaginal ultrasound in 3 months to assess for change
options.rationale: Interval imaging is a strategy for an asymptomatic incidental finding, and this woman has bleeding, which is the symptom that demands tissue rather than surveillance. Three months of observation in a woman with an increased baseline risk of endometrial carcinoma is not a safe deferral. (Source: RANZCOG: Investigation of postmenopausal bleeding)

options.text: Perform a Pipelle endometrial biopsy in the clinic and stop there
options.rationale: Blind outpatient sampling has good sensitivity for diffuse endometrial pathology but samples only a fraction of the cavity, so it misses focal lesions. Tamoxifen produces polyps, focal hyperplasia and subendometrial cystic change specifically, which is the near miss to hold onto: an adequate Pipelle result does not exclude a focal lesion in this population. (Source: RANZCOG: Investigation of postmenopausal bleeding)

options.text: Stop tamoxifen and switch her to an aromatase inhibitor, then review
options.rationale: Changing endocrine therapy is a decision for her medical oncologist and may well follow, but it does not diagnose the cause of the bleeding she has already had. Stopping the drug removes the stimulus without addressing whatever has already developed in the cavity. (Source: RANZCOG: Investigation of postmenopausal bleeding)

options.text: Arrange hysteroscopy with directed biopsy regardless of the thickness
options.rationale: Tamoxifen causes subendometrial stromal change that thickens and distorts the ultrasound appearance without indicating malignancy, so measurement cannot triage these women and the 4 mm rule does not apply to them. Hysteroscopy allows the cavity to be inspected directly and any focal lesion sampled under vision, which is the only approach that reliably excludes carcinoma in a woman with bleeding on tamoxifen. (Source: RANZCOG: Investigation of postmenopausal bleeding)

explanation.summary: Postmenopausal bleeding carries roughly a 10 per cent risk of endometrial carcinoma and is investigated in every woman, with transvaginal ultrasound used first in most: an endometrial thickness of 4 mm or less has a high negative predictive value and allows conservative management, while anything thicker requires tissue. Tamoxifen breaks that pathway. It acts as a partial oestrogen agonist on the endometrium, raising the risk of polyps, hyperplasia and carcinoma several fold, and it produces subendometrial cystic atrophy that inflates the measured thickness in women with entirely benign endometrium. As a result, ultrasound measurement in tamoxifen users has poor specificity and cannot be used to avoid sampling. Because the pathology tamoxifen produces is characteristically focal, blind sampling is also inadequate, and hysteroscopy with directed biopsy becomes the investigation of choice.
key_points: Postmenopausal bleeding always requires investigation, with about a 10 per cent cancer rate
The 4 mm endometrial thickness threshold is validated only in women not taking tamoxifen
Tamoxifen causes subendometrial cystic change that inflates the measurement without indicating malignancy
Tamoxifen associated pathology is typically focal, so blind sampling can miss it
Hysteroscopy with directed biopsy is the investigation of choice in this group
explanation.pearls: Asymptomatic endometrial thickening on tamoxifen does not warrant screening ultrasound or biopsy, but any bleeding at all takes a woman on tamoxifen straight to hysteroscopy rather than through a thickness threshold.

sources.label: eviQ: Tamoxifen in early breast cancer

subtopic_detail: Haemoptysis with irregular bleeding months after a term birth as metastatic gestational trophoblastic neoplasia
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar seeing a 34 year old woman with three weeks of breathlessness on climbing stairs and several episodes of coughing up bright red blood. She gave birth to a healthy baby at term 5 months ago.

She stopped breastfeeding at 3 months and has had irregular vaginal bleeding since about 6 weeks postpartum, which she attributed to her periods returning. She is a non smoker and has had no recent travel or immobility.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, SpO2 95 percent in room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Chest clear on auscultation, no calf swelling or tenderness, uterus not palpable abdominally, small amount of dark blood at the cervical os on speculum examination
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 98 g/L (115 to 155), white cell count 7.4 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0), platelets 246 x10^9/L (150 to 400), chest radiograph shows four rounded opacities up to 25 mm in both lung fields

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Measure the serum beta hCG and refer to a trophoblastic disease centre
options.rationale: Persistent abnormal bleeding after any pregnancy, including a normal term birth, with pulmonary nodules and haemoptysis is metastatic gestational trophoblastic neoplasia until beta hCG says otherwise, and the hormone is both the diagnostic test and the tumour marker used for staging and monitoring. Referral matters because these tumours are highly chemosensitive and cure rates approach 100 per cent with appropriate specialist treatment. (Source: RANZCOG: Gestational trophoblastic disease)

options.text: Arrange a computed tomography pulmonary angiogram and anticoagulate
options.rationale: Pulmonary embolism is a reasonable thought in a postpartum woman with breathlessness and haemoptysis, but discrete rounded pulmonary opacities are metastases rather than the peripheral wedge shaped infarcts of embolism, and there is no risk factor or calf finding. Anticoagulating a woman with vascular metastases and ongoing vaginal bleeding risks major haemorrhage. (Source: RANZCOG: Gestational trophoblastic disease)

options.text: Refer for bronchoscopy and biopsy of the largest pulmonary opacity
options.rationale: Biopsy of trophoblastic metastases is specifically hazardous because the lesions are highly vascular and bleed catastrophically, and it is unnecessary when a blood test makes the diagnosis. This is one of the few settings where tissue confirmation is actively avoided in favour of a tumour marker. (Source: RANZCOG: Gestational trophoblastic disease)

options.text: Treat as community acquired pneumonia with oral amoxicillin and review
options.rationale: Pneumonia produces fever, focal consolidation and abnormal auscultation rather than multiple discrete rounded opacities in an afebrile woman with a clear chest. Antibiotic treatment delays the diagnosis by the days or weeks it takes to demonstrate no response. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Arrange a computed tomography scan of the chest, abdomen and pelvis
options.rationale: Cross sectional imaging forms part of staging once the diagnosis is established, so it is a later step rather than a wrong one. Ordering it first delays a result available within hours from a single tube of blood, and the imaging alone would not distinguish trophoblastic metastases from other secondaries. (Source: RANZCOG: Gestational trophoblastic disease)

explanation.summary: Gestational trophoblastic neoplasia can follow any pregnancy event, and although the risk after a complete hydatidiform mole is highest, roughly a quarter of cases of choriocarcinoma follow a normal term birth. The clinical trap is that the antecedent pregnancy was uneventful, so nobody is monitoring beta hCG and the persistent bleeding is attributed to resumption of menstruation or retained products. Metastatic spread is haematogenous and pulmonary in most cases, giving rounded nodules and haemoptysis, with the vagina, liver and brain the next most common sites. Diagnosis rests on beta hCG rather than tissue, since biopsy of these very vascular lesions can cause life threatening haemorrhage, and treatment at a specialist centre with single agent or combination chemotherapy achieves cure in almost all women while preserving fertility.
key_points: Trophoblastic neoplasia can follow any pregnancy, including a normal term birth
Persistent postpartum bleeding beyond the expected period warrants a beta hCG measurement
Pulmonary metastases present as rounded nodules with haemoptysis and mimic embolism or infection
Diagnosis is made on beta hCG; biopsy of vascular metastases risks catastrophic bleeding
Cure rates approach 100 per cent with specialist chemotherapy, with fertility usually preserved
explanation.pearls: Any woman of reproductive age with unexplained metastatic disease should have a beta hCG measured before biopsy, because choriocarcinoma is curable, is diagnosed on the marker alone, and bleeds dangerously when sampled.

sources.label: Cancer Council Australia: Gestational trophoblastic neoplasia

subtopic_detail: Anticoagulation choice in early pregnancy for a mechanical mitral valve prosthesis on low dose warfarin
stem:
You are the obstetric physician registrar seeing a 32 year old woman at 6 weeks in her first pregnancy. She had a mechanical bileaflet mitral valve replacement 4 years ago for rheumatic valve disease and takes warfarin 4 mg daily with a target international normalised ratio of 3.0.

Her INR has been in range at every check for the past year. She has read online that warfarin harms babies and has already missed last night's dose. She has no bleeding, no breathlessness and no palpitations.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 82 beats per minute, blood pressure 110/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 percent in room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Crisp mechanical first heart sound with no murmur, chest clear, no peripheral oedema, no signs of embolism
data_table.Investigations: INR 2.4 today, full blood count and creatinine within normal limits, transthoracic echocardiogram 4 months ago showed normal prosthetic gradients and preserved left ventricular function, beta hCG consistent with dates

lead_in: What is the most appropriate anticoagulation plan for the first trimester?

options.text: Switch to therapeutic enoxaparin now and resume warfarin at 12 weeks
options.rationale: Substituting low molecular weight heparin through weeks 6 to 12 is an accepted alternative and removes the embryopathy risk, but it carries a higher rate of valve thrombosis than warfarin and demands anti Xa monitoring with dose adjustment at least every fortnight. It is the preferred option when the warfarin requirement exceeds 5 mg daily, because embryopathy risk climbs steeply above that dose, and this woman takes 4 mg. (Source: RANZCOG: Cardiac disease in pregnancy)

options.text: Continue warfarin at the current dose with weekly INR measurement
options.rationale: Warfarin embryopathy risk is dose dependent and falls below roughly 3 per cent when the daily requirement is 5 mg or less, while warfarin gives the lowest rate of valve thrombosis of any regimen, and a mitral prosthesis carries a higher thrombotic risk than an aortic one. Continuing it with frequent INR monitoring therefore gives the best combined maternal and foetal outcome in this woman, and the missed dose needs to be addressed today rather than allowed to continue. (Source: RANZCOG: Cardiac disease in pregnancy)

options.text: Switch to therapeutic enoxaparin for the whole of the pregnancy
options.rationale: Heparin throughout pregnancy avoids all foetal drug exposure and is the choice when a woman declines warfarin after counselling, but it carries the highest valve thrombosis rate of the accepted strategies, with reported maternal mortality in registries. Choosing it by default rather than by informed preference trades a small foetal risk for a substantially larger maternal one. (Source: RANZCOG: Cardiac disease in pregnancy)

options.text: Continue warfarin and add aspirin 100 mg daily until she delivers
options.rationale: Adding an antiplatelet agent to therapeutic warfarin is reserved for a prosthesis that has thrombosed or embolised despite adequate anticoagulation, and this valve has functioned normally with in range INRs for a year. The addition increases bleeding risk at delivery without addressing the question being asked. (Source: RANZCOG: Cardiac disease in pregnancy)

options.text: Switch to unfractionated heparin infusion and admit for monitoring
options.rationale: Intravenous unfractionated heparin has a role around delivery and in the peri-procedural period because it is short acting and reversible, but it is impractical as a first trimester strategy and inpatient care for 6 weeks is neither feasible nor safer. Unfractionated heparin also carries higher rates of osteoporosis and heparin induced thrombocytopenia with prolonged use. (Source: RANZCOG: Cardiac disease in pregnancy)

explanation.summary: A mechanical valve in pregnancy is one of the genuinely difficult trade-offs in obstetric medicine, because every available strategy harms either the mother or the foetus and the choice turns on quantities rather than principles. Pregnancy is prothrombotic, so anticoagulation cannot be interrupted, and valve thrombosis in pregnancy carries high maternal mortality. Warfarin crosses the placenta and causes an embryopathy of nasal hypoplasia and stippled epiphyses when taken between about 6 and 12 weeks, but the risk is strongly dose dependent and is low at daily doses of 5 mg or less, which is why guidelines separate women by dose rather than treating warfarin as uniformly unacceptable. Low molecular weight heparin removes the foetal exposure but consistently produces more valve thrombosis, in part because dosing is difficult to maintain as pregnancy alters clearance, and anti Xa monitoring with regular dose adjustment is mandatory if it is used. Direct oral anticoagulants are contraindicated with mechanical valves in and out of pregnancy.
key_points: Warfarin embryopathy risk is dose dependent and low at 5 mg daily or less
Warfarin gives the lowest valve thrombosis rate of the available regimens
Low molecular weight heparin removes foetal exposure but increases maternal thrombotic risk
Mitral prostheses carry higher thrombotic risk than aortic prostheses
Direct oral anticoagulants are contraindicated with any mechanical valve
explanation.pearls: Warfarin must be replaced by heparin from around 36 weeks, because a warfarinised foetus is anticoagulated at birth and vaginal delivery risks intracranial haemorrhage; an unplanned labour on warfarin is an indication for caesarean birth after maternal reversal.

sources.label: European Society of Cardiology: Cardiovascular diseases during pregnancy

subtopic_detail: Fitness to drive advice for a commercial vehicle driver commencing a sedating antipsychotic
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 44 year old man with schizophrenia whose olanzapine was increased three days ago after a relapse of persecutory beliefs. He is settling well and wants to return to work on Monday.

He drives a semi-trailer interstate and holds a commercial vehicle licence. He tells you he feels groggy until about lunchtime each day and has been sleeping 11 hours. He asks you not to write anything that might cost him his job, and says he will simply drink more coffee.

data_table.Mental state: Residual persecutory beliefs held with reduced conviction, no command hallucinations, no thoughts of harming himself or others, insight partial, cognition grossly intact but subjectively slowed
data_table.Examination: Mild psychomotor slowing, no parkinsonism, no akathisia, blood pressure 118/76 mmHg with no postural drop
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, urea and electrolytes, liver function tests and fasting glucose within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate course of action?

options.text: Clear him to drive as his psychotic symptoms have improved on treatment
options.rationale: Fitness to drive depends on the effect of both the illness and its treatment on the capacity to drive safely, not on symptomatic improvement alone. Daytime sedation persisting until midday is itself disqualifying for a driver of a heavy vehicle. (Source: Austroads: Assessing Fitness to Drive)

options.text: Notify the driver licensing authority today without telling the patient
options.rationale: Reporting to the licensing authority is a step taken when a patient continues to drive against advice and poses a genuine risk, and in most Australian jurisdictions the practitioner is permitted rather than obliged to report. Doing so covertly, before advising him and giving him the chance to comply, damages the therapeutic relationship and skips the step that usually resolves the problem. (Source: Austroads: Assessing Fitness to Drive)

options.text: Advise him not to drive, document the advice and arrange review
options.rationale: The treating doctor's duty is to assess fitness against the commercial standard, which is substantially stricter than the private one, to advise the patient directly of the consequences for driving, and to record that advice in the notes. Reassessment once the sedation has settled and the illness is stable allows a considered decision about return to commercial driving, with a conditional licence if appropriate. (Source: Austroads: Assessing Fitness to Drive)

options.text: Halve the olanzapine dose so that he can return to driving on Monday
options.rationale: Reducing an effective antipsychotic dose days after a relapse to meet an occupational deadline risks a further relapse, which carries a far greater driving risk than sedation does. Treatment decisions should not be reverse engineered from a return to work date. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Leave the decision to him since he knows his own tolerance to the drug
options.rationale: Insight is partial and the patient has already proposed managing residual sedation with caffeine, so his self-assessment is not a reliable basis for a decision affecting public safety. The assessment of fitness to drive is a clinical judgement the doctor is required to make and communicate. (Source: Austroads: Assessing Fitness to Drive)

explanation.summary: Fitness to drive in Australia is governed by the Austroads standards, which set two tiers, with commercial vehicle drivers held to a considerably stricter standard than private drivers because of the vehicle's mass, the hours driven and the consequences of a crash. For psychiatric illness the standard considers the illness itself, including symptoms that impair judgement, concentration or reality testing, and the effects of treatment, notably sedation, extrapyramidal effects and postural hypotension. The treating doctor assesses fitness, advises the patient of any restriction and documents that advice, while the licensing authority makes the licensing decision, often with a conditional licence subject to periodic review. Most jurisdictions give practitioners a discretionary power, with statutory protection, to notify the authority when a patient who has been advised not to drive continues to do so, and the Northern Territory and South Australia impose specific reporting obligations. Advising the patient first is not merely courteous but usually effective, since most people comply once the risk is explained.
key_points: Commercial driver standards are substantially stricter than private driver standards
Both the illness and the sedating effects of its treatment are assessed
The doctor assesses and advises; the licensing authority decides the licence
Advice not to drive must be documented in the clinical record
Notification is generally discretionary and follows continued driving against advice
explanation.pearls: Write the words used and the date in the notes when advising a patient not to drive, because that documented advice is what protects both the patient and the practitioner if a crash occurs, and it is the precondition for any later notification to the licensing authority.

subtopic_detail: Antidepressant associated sexual dysfunction in sustained remission where the agent rather than the treatment is changed
stem:
You are the general practice registrar reviewing a 34 year old man who has taken sertraline 100 mg daily for 14 months after a single severe depressive episode. His mood, sleep, appetite and concentration have been back to baseline for 8 months and he has returned to full time work.

Over that time he has found it takes far longer to reach orgasm and his interest in sex has dropped noticeably. This is causing tension with his partner and he says he is close to stopping the tablets himself. He has no erectile difficulty and no early morning erections have been lost.

data_table.Examination: Euthymic mood with reactive affect, no psychomotor change, no suicidal ideation, body mass index 25 kg/m2, normal secondary sexual characteristics and testicular examination
data_table.Investigations: Total testosterone 18 nmol/L (8 to 30), TSH 1.6 mIU/L (0.4 to 4.0), fasting glucose 4.8 mmol/L (3.0 to 5.4), HbA1c 33 mmol/mol (less than 42)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Switch to an antidepressant with a lower sexual adverse effect profile
options.rationale: Sexual dysfunction affects a large minority of people on serotonergic antidepressants, rarely resolves with time, and is a leading reason for unilateral discontinuation and subsequent relapse. Switching to an agent with lower serotonergic burden, such as mirtazapine, agomelatine or vortioxetine, preserves treatment of the illness while addressing the adverse effect that is about to end it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Advise weekend drug holidays from sertraline before planned intimacy
options.rationale: Planned omission of doses has been described with shorter acting agents, but it produces discontinuation symptoms, risks destabilising mood, and makes intimacy a scheduled clinical event. It also teaches intermittent adherence in a man already inclined to stop. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Continue sertraline unchanged and reassure him this resolves with time
options.rationale: Tolerance to sexual adverse effects develops in only a minority and usually within the first weeks, not after 14 months of treatment. Reassurance that is not borne out by the evidence is likely to be followed by the abrupt self discontinuation he has already flagged. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Stop sertraline now given that he has been well for eight months
options.rationale: After a first severe episode, treatment is generally continued for at least 6 to 12 months of full remission before a planned taper, and abrupt cessation of sertraline also causes discontinuation symptoms. Stopping in response to an adverse effect, rather than as a planned decision, removes protection from relapse without any attempt to keep him treated. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Add sildenafil 50 mg to be taken before intercourse and review
options.rationale: Phosphodiesterase inhibitors improve erectile function and have some evidence in antidepressant associated dysfunction in men, but his difficulty is delayed orgasm and reduced desire with erectile function preserved. The near pair worth separating is that sildenafil addresses erection, not libido or orgasmic latency. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

explanation.summary: Sexual dysfunction is among the most common and least discussed adverse effects of serotonergic antidepressants, reported in roughly 40 to 60 per cent of treated patients when asked directly, and it affects desire, arousal and orgasm in both men and women. It is frequently mistaken for a residual symptom of depression, so the sequence matters: dysfunction that predates treatment and improves as mood recovers is illness, while dysfunction that appears or worsens once mood has remitted is drug effect. Options are dose reduction, switching to an agent with lower serotonergic burden, augmentation, or adjunctive treatment targeting the specific difficulty. The clinical cost of leaving it unaddressed is high, because unilateral discontinuation in the first year is a major driver of relapse.
key_points: Ask directly, because patients rarely volunteer sexual adverse effects
Dysfunction emerging after mood remission points to drug effect rather than residual illness
Tolerance develops in only a minority and usually early
Mirtazapine, agomelatine and vortioxetine carry lower sexual adverse effect burden
Unaddressed dysfunction drives unilateral discontinuation and relapse
explanation.pearls: Check whether sexual difficulty preceded the antidepressant: a man whose libido fell during the depressive episode and has not recovered after remission needs a switch, not reassurance, and a testosterone measured in the morning when hypogonadism is suspected.

sources.label: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline

subtopic_detail: Herbal preparation interacting with a serotonergic antidepressant and hormonal contraception
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 29 year old woman who has taken escitalopram 10 mg daily for 7 months for a depressive episode and uses a combined oral contraceptive pill. Three weeks ago she bought a herbal preparation from a health food shop to help her mood and has taken it daily since.

Over the past week she has felt restless and jittery, has been sweating through her shirts, and her hands shake when she holds a coffee. She has also had two episodes of unexpected vaginal bleeding, which has not happened before on the pill.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 128/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 percent in room air, temperature 37.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Fine tremor of the outstretched hands, brisk reflexes with three beats of inducible ankle clonus, pupils 5 mm and reactive, no rigidity, alert and fully oriented
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 180 units/L (30 to 200), urea and electrolytes and liver function tests within normal limits, beta hCG negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Stop escitalopram and continue the herbal preparation and the pill
options.rationale: Stopping the prescribed antidepressant while continuing the agent that precipitated the problem leaves the serotonergic load partly in place, since the herbal preparation is itself serotonergic, and abandons treatment of her depression. It also leaves the contraceptive failure risk entirely unaddressed. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Stop the herbal preparation and review her within 48 hours
options.rationale: St John's wort has serotonergic activity and combining it with a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor produces mild to moderate serotonin toxicity, with the tremor, hyperreflexia, inducible clonus, diaphoresis and low grade fever seen here. It is also a potent inducer of cytochrome P450 3A4 and P-glycoprotein, which accelerates oestrogen and progestogen metabolism and explains the breakthrough bleeding, so stopping it addresses both problems and short interval review confirms resolution. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Continue all three and arrange review in 4 weeks as planned
options.rationale: Serotonin toxicity exists on a spectrum and mild features can progress to hyperthermia, rigidity and rhabdomyolysis if the serotonergic load continues. Four weeks of continued exposure also means four weeks of unreliable contraception. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Add cyproheptadine 8 mg orally and continue current medication
options.rationale: Cyproheptadine is a serotonin antagonist used in moderate to severe serotonin toxicity that does not settle with withdrawal of the offending agents and supportive care. Giving it while the precipitant continues treats the symptom and leaves the cause running. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Increase the escitalopram dose to 20 mg daily to control symptoms
options.rationale: Restlessness can reflect undertreated anxiety, but increasing the serotonergic dose in a patient with clonus, tremor and diaphoresis escalates the toxicity that is producing the symptoms. Hyperreflexia with inducible clonus is the physical sign that distinguishes serotonin toxicity from anxiety. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: St John's wort is sold without prescription and is frequently not disclosed unless patients are asked specifically about complementary medicines, yet it is among the most interaction prone preparations in common use. Pharmacodynamically it is serotonergic and adds to the load of antidepressants, triptans, tramadol and other agents. Pharmacokinetically it induces cytochrome P450 3A4 and P-glycoprotein, lowering concentrations of hormonal contraceptives, warfarin, ciclosporin, some antiretrovirals, direct oral anticoagulants and many anticancer drugs, with contraceptive failure and transplant rejection both reported. Serotonin toxicity is diagnosed clinically using the Hunter criteria, in which spontaneous clonus, or inducible clonus with agitation or diaphoresis, is sufficient, and the cornerstone of treatment is withdrawing the serotonergic agents with supportive care.
key_points: Ask explicitly about complementary and over the counter preparations at every medication review
St John's wort is serotonergic and induces cytochrome P450 3A4 and P-glycoprotein
Contraceptive failure and breakthrough bleeding are recognised consequences of that induction
Hunter criteria rest on clonus, agitation, diaphoresis, tremor, hyperreflexia and hyperthermia
Withdrawal of the offending agents plus supportive care treats most cases
explanation.pearls: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome and serotonin toxicity are separated at the ankles: serotonin toxicity produces hyperreflexia and clonus that are more marked in the lower limbs, while neuroleptic malignant syndrome produces lead pipe rigidity with hyporeflexia and a markedly raised creatine kinase.

subtopic_detail: Blood injection injury phobia with vasovagal syncope requiring applied tension rather than anxiolysis
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 22 year old nursing student who needs immunisations before her first clinical placement in 5 weeks. She tells you she has fainted at every blood test since she was 14 and once hit her head on a desk after a school vaccination.

She describes feeling hot and sweaty when she sees the needle, then her vision greys out and she wakes on the floor. She has no difficulty with heights, enclosed spaces, flying or public speaking, and is otherwise confident and outgoing.

data_table.Examination: Cardiovascular examination normal with no postural drop in blood pressure, electrocardiogram sinus rhythm with normal intervals, no neurological abnormality
data_table.Mental state: Euthymic, no generalised worry, no panic attacks outside medical settings, no avoidance of any other situation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Prescribe diazepam 5 mg orally one hour before each procedure
options.rationale: Benzodiazepine premedication reduces anticipatory anxiety but does not prevent the vasovagal reflex, and by blunting the situation it prevents the extinction learning that exposure depends on. It also introduces sedation and dependence risk in a student who will face needles throughout her career. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Prescribe propranolol 10 mg orally one hour before each procedure
options.rationale: Beta blockade attenuates the tachycardia of performance anxiety, but the physiology here is the opposite: an initial sympathetic surge followed by parasympathetic overactivity with bradycardia and hypotension. Blocking sympathetic tone can therefore make the faint more likely rather than less. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Commence sertraline 50 mg daily and review her in four weeks
options.rationale: Antidepressants have a role in panic disorder, social anxiety disorder and generalised anxiety disorder, and are not first line for a specific phobia confined to one narrow stimulus. This woman has no anxiety symptoms outside medical settings and no other avoidance. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Advise that she lie supine for all future blood tests and stop there
options.rationale: Supine positioning is a sensible adjunct that reduces injury from a faint, and it is part of good practice rather than a treatment. Offered alone it manages the consequence while leaving the phobia and the fainting reflex untouched, and she will still faint during placements when she is the one holding the needle. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Refer for applied tension training with graded exposure therapy
options.rationale: Blood injection injury phobia is unique among the phobias in producing a diphasic vasovagal response with syncope, so the specific treatment is applied tension, in which the patient repeatedly tenses large muscle groups to raise blood pressure and abort the faint, combined with graded exposure. It is effective in a small number of sessions and gives her a portable skill for a career in which she will encounter needles constantly. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Specific phobias are highly prevalent, usually begin in childhood and are treated with graded exposure, which has the strongest evidence base of any psychological intervention for anxiety. Blood injection injury phobia is set apart by its physiology: unlike other phobias, which produce sustained sympathetic arousal, it produces an initial rise in heart rate and blood pressure followed by an abrupt parasympathetic swing with bradycardia, hypotension and syncope in around 70 per cent of sufferers. That is why the standard treatment adds applied tension, a technique of tensing the arms, torso and legs in cycles to raise blood pressure at the moment the faint would otherwise occur. The clinical stakes extend beyond the phobia itself, since avoidance leads people to defer blood tests, vaccinations, dental treatment and pregnancy care.
key_points: Blood injection injury phobia uniquely produces a diphasic response ending in vasovagal syncope
Applied tension raises blood pressure and prevents the faint, unlike relaxation training
Graded exposure is the core treatment for all specific phobias
Benzodiazepines blunt exposure learning and do not prevent the vasovagal reflex
Untreated phobia leads to avoidance of vaccination, blood tests and antenatal care
explanation.pearls: Teach applied tension as 10 to 15 second cycles of tensing the arms, trunk and legs until the face feels flushed, repeated five times with 20 second breaks, and have the patient start the cycles at the first sign of warmth or lightheadedness rather than after the vision greys.

subtopic_detail: Antidepressant selection in an older woman with weight loss, insomnia and previous drug induced hyponatraemia
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 78 year old woman who has been persistently low, tearful and uninterested in her craft group since her husband died 14 months ago. She has lost 6 kg without trying, pushes her meals around the plate, and lies awake for two hours before she gets to sleep.

Last year a trial of sertraline was stopped after 3 weeks when her sodium fell to 126 mmol/L, which corrected within a fortnight of ceasing it. She takes no regular medications, lives alone and has no thoughts of harming herself.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 19 kg/m2, no postural hypotension, Mini-Mental State Examination 28 out of 30, no focal neurological signs, thyroid not palpable
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 139 mmol/L (135 to 145), potassium 4.2 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.2), creatinine 78 micromol/L (45 to 90), eGFR 62 mL/min/1.73m2, TSH 2.4 mIU/L (0.4 to 4.0), haemoglobin 128 g/L (115 to 155), B12 and folate within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate pharmacological treatment?

options.text: Re-trial sertraline 25 mg daily with sodium checked at one week
options.rationale: Rechallenge with the same drug class after a documented syndrome of inappropriate antidiuresis carries a high rate of recurrence, and older women are the group at greatest risk. Monitoring detects the problem rather than preventing it, and a second hyponatraemic episode delays effective treatment further. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Commence venlafaxine 37.5 mg daily and review her in two weeks
options.rationale: Serotonin noradrenaline reuptake inhibitors carry a comparable or slightly higher risk of hyponatraemia than selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, so this does not avoid the problem that stopped the last trial. Venlafaxine also raises blood pressure at higher doses and causes prominent discontinuation symptoms. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Commence amitriptyline 25 mg at night for sleep and appetite
options.rationale: Tricyclic antidepressants do help sleep and appetite, but the anticholinergic burden causes confusion, urinary retention, constipation and falls in older people, and they are cardiotoxic in overdose. They are also associated with hyponatraemia, so the specific problem being avoided is not solved. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Commence mirtazapine 15 mg at night and monitor weight and mood
options.rationale: Mirtazapine's antihistaminergic and 5-HT2 and 5-HT3 antagonist actions improve sleep onset and stimulate appetite, which directly target the weight loss and initial insomnia that dominate her presentation. It carries a lower reported rate of hyponatraemia than serotonin reuptake inhibitors, making it the rational choice after a documented episode. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Prescribe temazepam 10 mg at night and review the mood in a month
options.rationale: A hypnotic treats one symptom of a depressive episode while leaving the illness untreated, and benzodiazepines in this age group increase falls, hip fracture and confusion. Sleep disturbance driven by depression improves when the depression is treated. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Depression in older adults is frequently missed because it presents with somatic complaints, weight loss, poor sleep and apparent cognitive slowing rather than expressed sadness, and it must be distinguished from prolonged grief disorder, dementia and organic causes such as hypothyroidism and B12 deficiency. Antidepressant associated hyponatraemia is a class effect of serotonergic drugs, appears within the first few weeks, and is commonest in older women, in those on diuretics and in those with low body weight, so a documented episode should steer subsequent choices rather than being treated as a one-off. Mirtazapine is often chosen in this situation because of its lower reported rate of hyponatraemia and because its sedating and appetite stimulating effects are therapeutic rather than merely tolerable in an underweight patient with insomnia. Starting low and going slow remains the rule, with the caveat that the dose must eventually reach a therapeutic level and be given an adequate trial of 4 to 6 weeks.
key_points: Older adults present with somatic symptoms, weight loss and poor sleep rather than stated sadness
Antidepressant hyponatraemia is a serotonergic class effect appearing in the first weeks
Older women, low body weight and concurrent diuretics are the main risk factors
Mirtazapine carries a lower reported hyponatraemia rate and helps sleep and appetite
Exclude hypothyroidism, B12 deficiency and anaemia before attributing symptoms to mood
explanation.pearls: Mirtazapine is more sedating at 15 mg than at 30 mg, because noradrenergic transmission at higher doses offsets the antihistaminergic effect, so a patient complaining of daytime grogginess on 15 mg is often better on 30 mg rather than less.

sources.label: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline
